n: The book of Job opens like a story: a man in a land called Uz who is blameless and devoted to God. The book will wrestle with a hard question — why do good people suffer? The Lord later reminded Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail of Job’s trials.

f.g: A region probably east or southeast of Israel, toward Edom or northern Arabia (Lamentations 4:21).
Hebrew tam — whole, blameless, of complete integrity; not “never made a mistake.”
Avoided, turned away from.

n: Job has seven sons and three daughters. Seven and three were numbers of completeness — his family is perfectly blessed.
He is enormously wealthy in livestock and servants — the richest man in the East. Wealth in that culture was measured in animals.

f.g: Pairs of oxen used for plowing.
Female donkeys, valued for milk and breeding.
The peoples east of Israel, known for their wisdom (1 Kings 4:30).

n: His grown children take turns hosting feasts, and the brothers include their sisters. It is a picture of a happy, close family.

f.g: Each on his own day, perhaps birthdays.

n: After each round of feasts, Job rises early to offer sacrifices for each child, just in case they had sinned in their hearts. He acts as the family’s priest, as patriarchs did before the law of Moses.

f.g: Had them ritually purified.
The Hebrew says “blessed God,” a polite substitute scribes used to avoid writing “curse God.”

n: The scene shifts to heaven, where the “sons of God” — heavenly beings — present themselves before the Lord. Among them comes “the Satan,” meaning “the adversary” or accuser.

f.g: Hebrew ha-satan, “the adversary” or “the accuser.”

n: The Lord asks where he has been. Satan answers that he has been roaming the earth — restless, watching, looking for faults.

f.w: going to and fro in the earth

n: The Lord points out Job with obvious pride: there is no one like him on earth. The Lord calls him “my servant,” a title of honor.

f.g: Literally “Have you set your heart on” — have you noticed.

n: Satan’s challenge is the question of the whole book: does Job serve God for nothing? In other words, is his goodness real, or is it just a good deal?

f.g: For nothing — without reward or self-interest.

n: Satan argues that God has put a protective hedge around Job and blessed everything he does. Of course Job is faithful — it pays.

f.g: A protective fence — divine protection.

n: Take it all away, Satan says, and Job will curse you to your face. He claims that no one loves God freely.

f.g: Strike his possessions.

n: The Lord allows Satan to test Job’s possessions but not to harm Job himself. Satan has power only within limits God sets.

f.w: only upon himself put not forth thine hand

n: Back on earth, on a festive day while Job’s children are feasting at the oldest brother’s house, disaster begins.
A messenger arrives with news about Job’s plowing oxen and the donkeys grazing nearby.
Raiders from Sheba steal the animals and kill the servants. Only one survives to bring the news.

f.g: Raiders from Sheba, in southern Arabia.

f.w: I only am escaped alone to tell thee
f.g: This refrain repeats four times, like hammer blows.

n: Before he finishes, a second messenger reports that “the fire of God” — likely lightning — has burned up the sheep and the shepherds.

f.g: Probably lightning; compare 1 Kings 18:38.

n: A third messenger arrives: Chaldean raiders in three groups have stolen the camels and killed the servants.

f.g: Raiders from Mesopotamia; long before they became the Babylonian empire.
Three raiding parties.

n: Then the fourth messenger comes with the worst news of all, about Job’s children at their brother’s house.
A violent wind from the desert struck the house, and it collapsed on them; all his children are dead. In one day Job loses everything, from his wealth to his beloved family.

f.w: a great wind from the wilderness
f.g: Probably a desert whirlwind striking all four corners.
Hebrew can mean “young people,” including his daughters.

n: Job tears his robe and shaves his head — signs of grief — and falls to the ground. But in his grief, he worships.

f.g: Tore his outer robe in mourning.

n: Job’s famous words: I was born with nothing, and I will leave with nothing. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away — blessed be His name. His faith is real.

f.w: Naked came I out of my mother's womb

f.g: There — to the earth, the “mother” of all.

f.w: blessed be the name of the LORD

n: Through all this, Job did not sin or accuse God of wrongdoing. Satan’s prediction has failed.

f.g: Blamed God for wrongdoing.

f.w: In all this Job sinned not
